20003-the-infernal-marriage:
Disraeli's The Infernal Marriage is a satirical tale of gods and modern manners. It first appeared within his novel Henrietta Temple in 1837. Lady Ceres is promised to calm with time in its dialogue. What is done cannot be undone, the speaker soothes. A winter residence among the gods is even desirable, she is told. She may pay a visit by then, he predicts. Olympus here behaves like a London drawing room.

The tale retells Proserpine's marriage to Pluto as society comedy. Disraeli stuffs heaven with dowagers, dandies, and political talk. It is classical myth recut as a fashionable novel. Young Disraeli delighted in such blasphemous elegance. The piece shows his wit before Parliament tamed it. Readers meet the dandy-satirist in pure form.
20336-the-miraculous-revenge:
The Miraculous Revenge is a tale of Ireland, love, and a long-sought mystery. A man recalls first seeing a woman he hoped might solve his quest. On this night he watches and hears her only for that bygone hope. He applauds her generously as the curtain falls on her act.

Then he sups at a restaurant, returns to his hotel, and tries to read. Loneliness still sits with him despite the evening's bright show. Revenge in Irish tales often turns on wit, faith, and old wrongs. Readers get a moody, comic tale in the Irish storytelling vein.
20473-grace-harlowe-s-third-year-at-over:
In Grace Harlowe's Third Year at Overton College, published in 1914, Grace and her friends are deep into college life. The Eight Originals, as the friends call themselves, face a September parting. Miriam Nesbit and seven of the group spend a last evening on the Harlowes' wide veranda.

It is a warm night, and the talk turns on the day to come. The next morning will scatter the friends to their separate duties. The Grace Harlowe books followed their heroine year by year, and this volume catches the mix of freedom and farewell that college readers knew well.
20474-grace-harlowe-s-fourth-year-at-ove:
Grace Harlowe's Fourth Year at Overton College, published in 1914, brings Grace and the Eight Originals to their senior year. College rooms, parties, and old friendships crowd the chapters. Ruth and Grace plan one more gathering in a room they both know is too small.

Ruth remembers a Hallowe'en party in that same room the year before. It held eighteen girls one night, she says, and what a time they had squeezing in. The senior-year book closes Grace's college course with the warmth and loyalty that made the series a staple for girl readers.
20485-the-lunatic-at-large:
J. Storer Clouston's The Lunatic at Large is a comic novel that begins, as its title warns, with an escape. Its early pages introduce a young professional man in some detail. He may be described as amiable-looking, with a little fair moustache and still less chin.

He has no practice to speak of, and a considerable quantity of unpaid bills. A man of such features and in such circumstances, the narrator says, invites temptation. Clouston sends his characters through mistaken identities and absurd chases, in the brisk farce style that made this one of his best-loved books.
20667-a-canyon-voyage:
F. S. Dellenbaugh's A Canyon Voyage, published in 1908, narrates the second Powell expedition down the Colorado River in 1871 and 1872. Dellenbaugh went as a young artist and mapmaker. His book, written years later, is the fullest personal account of that voyage through the Grand Canyon country.

His figures give the canyon's scale. The gorge drops near six thousand feet on the north side and over five thousand on the south. Its total length, counting the Marble Canyon division, runs 283 miles. Dellenbaugh made sketches in colour on the spot, and the narrative keeps a painter's eye.
21197-diego-collado-s-grammar-of-the-jap:
Diego Collado, a Spanish Dominican missionary, published his grammar of Japanese in Latin in 1632, one of the earliest European studies of the language. Richard L. Spear edited and translated it for the University of Kansas East Asian series. His introduction compares Collado's account with the grammar by João Rodrigues.

Spear explains Collado's framework for Japanese sounds, word forms, and sentence structure before the translation begins. The 1632 original, Ars Grammaticae Iaponicae Linguae, also circulates as a separate text. For students of language history, the book shows how missionaries first fitted Japanese into Latin grammar terms, and where that fit strained. The book is old, rare, and hard to find in print now.
21405-the-loss-of-the-royal-george:
Ben Truscott's father was boatswain of the Royal George, and W. H. G. Kingston tells her loss through Ben's eyes. The great ship carried over a hundred brass guns and flew an admiral's flag. She had been launched in 1756 and was a pride of the navy.

Her sinking takes only a few pages, and the heart of the tale lies elsewhere. A small child brought aboard by a lady survives, while the lady drowns. A crewman raises the boy, who makes a good career at sea. In the last chapter his true parents are found, and all ends well.
21514-gryll-grange:
Thomas Love Peacock's Gryll Grange, his last novel, is shown here in the 1896 Macmillan edition. George Saintsbury writes the preface, and F. H. Townsend draws the pictures. Chapter heads promise squires, vicars, and a lord with a taste for grand dinners.

Peacock packs talk on science, exams, music, and the press into a country-house tale. A rustic lover, a thunderstorm, and the lottery of marriage stir the plot. Lord Curryfin's Siberian dinners and social tedium get sharp, funny treatment. The book is talk at its most sparkling, from a master of the comic dialogue novel.
21551-the-little-savage:
A boy grows up near alone on a rocky island in Captain Marryat's The Little Savage, published in 1848. His one companion, a morose and gloomy man, drags him over hard climbs and treats him unkindly. It was Marryat's twenty-sixth book, finished after his death by kin.

The tale was meant for children, and its religious tone sets it apart from Marryat's other works. Shipwreck, survival, and a child's slow schooling in faith and feeling drive the plot. Marryat died the year it appeared, leaving the book as a gentler last word. Its island scenes still hold young readers fast.
21639-when-patty-went-to-college:
Jean Webster sends Patty to a women's college in When Patty Went to College, published in 1903. Patty's roommate Priscilla drags pillows and curtains from a dry-goods box at term's start. Fifty girls, Patty jokes, have already begged the janitor Peters for his hammer.

Chapters treat an early fright, a question of ethics, and the elusive Kate Ferris. Patty comforts friends, pursues old English, and meets a bishop with grace. C. D. Williams draws the pictures, from Patty's portrait onward. Webster later won fame with Daddy-Long-Legs, and her wit and warmth are already here in full.
21701-the-settler-and-the-savage:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote adventure novels for young readers in the nineteenth century, and this one is set in South Africa. The story opens on the great dry plains called the karroo in the first quarter of that century. A young rider named Charlie Considine is lost there with his horse, Rob Roy, short of water under a hot sun.

From that hard start, the tale follows Charlie among settlers and the wild country around them. Ballantyne had a gift for plain, fast storytelling, and he fills the pages with travel, danger, and close escapes. Readers get a vivid picture of frontier life in southern Africa as English settlers saw it, told as a boy's own adventure.
21866-the-gundungurra-language:
An Australian Aboriginal language is set down on paper in R. H. Mathews's study of Gundungurra, read before a learned society in October 1901. The Gundungurra and Dharrook peoples held country from the Hawkesbury River to Mount Victoria and south to Berrima and Goulburn. Mathews notes features not before reported in Australia. Nouns, verbs, and pronouns carry rich inflections, and the first person has two forms each of dual and plural.

He spells every word phonetically in nineteen English letters and explains each sound. The little word for yes, ngee, opens his notes on the tricky ng. Such papers, dry as they look, preserve languages under heavy pressure. Mathews's record remains a source for Gundungurra descendants and linguists alike.
21995-philosophy-and-religion-six-lectur:
Materialism is impossible, argues Hastings Rashdall in Philosophy and Religion, six lectures delivered at Cambridge and published in 1909. Rashdall, fellow of New College, Oxford, begins with mind and matter. All we know of matter, he says, implies mind: color and sound plainly, but solidity and size no less. This was Berkeley's great discovery, though Berkeley blurred parts of it.

If matter cannot exist apart from mind, Rashdall reasons, there must be a universal mind in which all things exist: God. Yet he grants that theism is possible without idealism. The lectures move with a tutor's patience from Spinoza and Spencer to faith. They show Edwardian Oxford philosophy at its clearest, arguing for religion on reason's own ground.
22001-pastoral-poems-by-nicholas-breton-:
Three Elizabethan pastoral poets share this slim booklet of 1906, third in the Pembroke Booklets series from Hull. Nicholas Breton (1558 to 1626) leads with his pastoral poems; Ben Jonson praised his work as the habit of true passion in perfect strains. George Wither (1588 to 1667) follows with selected poetry. Charles Lamb's praise heads his section: Wither first found poetry a present wealth, not only a hope after death.

William Browne of Tavistock closes the volume with his pastoral poetry. The editor warns that the fate of poets is uncertain, and these three survive but slowly in public interest. The edition was limited to two hundred fifty large-paper copies. It is a small act of rescue for the singing shepherds of England's golden age of verse.
22183-wilton-school-or-harry-campbell-s-:
Wilton School; or, Harry Campbell's Revenge is a school story told as a tale. It opens on a sad summer evening in a little farm by Wilton church. The low, dim parlour, panelled in oak, looks across the quiet churchyard. Lindens shade the gravel path, and sorrow sits inside despite the sweet weather without.

From that farm the tale sends Harry Campbell to Wilton School. Schoolboy honour, injury, and the hunger for revenge drive the plot. The book belongs to the early school-story kind, before the genre found its classic shape. Its moral is worked out through friendship and disgrace rather than games, which came later to rule such fiction.
22244-miss-pat-at-artemis-lodge:
Pemberton Ginther wrote Miss Pat at Artemis Lodge in 1917, one of her Miss Pat books for girls. Patricia and her friends have settled at Artemis Lodge, an art colony. The story opens in a flurry: the train is in, and Judith begs Elinor to watch one corner while she watches the other. Bruce has gone for a taxi so as not to lose a minute, and a beloved arrival is expected any second.

Studies, models, pranks, and friendships fill the girls' days at the lodge. Ginther writes bright boarding-house comedy with art-school trimmings. The Miss Pat series followed its heroine from school to art study and beyond. This volume shows the series at its sunniest.
22845-the-beauty-of-the-village:
One good workman carries The Beauty of the Village, a character sketch by Mary Russell Mitford. Her subject is a man of the old school. He served his employers faithfully, never thought his work beneath him, and filled every family role with credit. A big family grew up well under his care. Drink never drew him into a tavern once.

Mitford's title plays gently against expectations. The village beauty here is not a face but a life. Through one man's steady record she praises the unnoticed virtues that hold a parish together. The sketch is brief, warm, and exact. It shows why her village portraits were loved. She found the remarkable inside the ordinary and made readers see it too.
23242-laramie-holds-the-range:
Frank H. Spearman's Laramie Holds the Range, from 1921, is a western novel named for its hero. Its opening rides a train west. All day, a heavy train of sleeping cars has climbed the long rise from the river, across a dull stretch of treeless, short-grass plains.

Those plains run from the Missouri River to the mountains. Then the train stops again, almost without a sound. Spearman builds the West from such quiet details: distance, grass, and rail lines crossing empty country. Readers get a range story where the land itself sets the pace before Laramie takes hold of it.
291-the-golden-age:
Children ruled by aunts and uncles turn holidays into kingdoms in Kenneth Grahame's Golden Age. The prologue calls adults Olympians, kind to bodily needs but deaf to imagination. Aunts, uncles, and governesses stand far above the children's world.

Chapters follow a white-washed uncle, alarms and excursions, the finding of a princess, and the secret drawer. The Argonauts, the Roman road, and a falling out fill the year. Grahame writes childhood from inside, with wit and longing. The book preceded his Dream Days and Willows. Grahame's childhood tales influenced later writers of children's fantasy.
293-paul-prescott-s-charge:
Paul Prescott's dying father leaves him a charge: keep integrity and duty through every campaign of life. Horatio Alger Jr.'s Paul Prescott's Charge, second in the Campaign Series, follows Paul from a boarding school at Potowome through hardship. The preface states Alger's idea plainly.

Paul battles adverse circumstances, earns his way, and holds to his father's charge under discouragement. Alger dedicates the book to boys who remember that school. The story's moral energy made it a staple of boyhood reading. It shows Alger's formula at its most earnest. Alger's campaign moral gave generations of boys a model of steady duty.
351-of-human-bondage:
W. Somerset Maugham follows Philip Carey from a lonely childhood to adult life in this long novel. Philip, born with a club foot, loses his mother early and grows up under strict kin. He tries school, clerk work, art in Paris, and medicine in London, each path testing his pride and his need for love.

A cruel affair with a waitress named Mildred breaks his heart and his funds more than once, while steadier friends offer a saner path. Maugham writes in plain, steady prose, with little show. The book endures as a study of how a sensitive man learns to live with limits, and to want less yet feel more free.
375-an-occurrence-at-owl-creek-bridge:
Ambrose Bierce sets this short Civil War tale on a railroad bridge in northern Alabama. A Southern planter, Peyton Farquhar, stands bound with a rope round his neck, guarded by Federal soldiers. As the trap drops, his mind races through a vivid dream of escape, flight through woods, and a rush home to his wife.

Bierce times the dream with care, letting each sense sharpen as Farquhar runs. The final twist snaps the dream shut and restores the grim fact of the bridge. The story endures for its tight craft and its stark view of war, hope, and self-deceit in a few short pages.
439-the-vital-message:
Arthur Conan Doyle argues for spirit contact in this 1919 sequel to The New Revelation, written after the Great War. Doyle claims the war's vast loss opened minds to a new relation with the unseen. He sets out the evidence and the changes he expects in science, faith, and daily life.

Chapters treat the dawning light, the great argument, and the coming world, with notes on spirit photos and clairvoyance. Doyle writes with earnest conviction, as a public man pleading a cause. The book stands as a clear record of his later faith, and of a generation seeking comfort beyond the grave.
481-in-the-bishop-s-carriage:
Miriam Michelson tells of Nancy, a young pickpocket who poses as a Bryn Mawr girl to dodge police, in this brisk novel. After a theft at a station, Nancy slips into a bishop's carriage and talks her way into a new life among polite folk. Her thief friend Tom watches from the shadows, torn between love and the law.

Michelson writes in Nancy's quick, slangy voice, full of nerve and humor. Each chapter tests whether Nancy can keep her act, or fall back to the streets. The novel charms as a tale of disguise and second chances, where a sharp girl outwits both cops and society.
534-an-inland-voyage:
Robert Louis Stevenson recounts a canoe trip through Belgium and France in this early travel book. With his friend Cigarette, Stevenson paddles the Sambre and Oise canals, past Antwerp, Maubeuge, and Noyon, camping, portaging, and dining with canal folk. A preface jokes that a small book needs a large welcome.

Stevenson writes with light, witty prose, keen on rain, inns, and cathedral towns. The voyage is less about distance than about talk and temper on the water. The book charms as a young writer's ramble, where a canoe proves a fine lens for foreign life.
94-alexander-s-bridge:
Bartley Alexander builds great bridges and a great reputation, then risks both for an old love. Willa Cather's Alexander's Bridge, her first novel, follows the engineer between Boston, London, and the Canadian west. Professor Wilson watches his friend's rise with quiet doubt.

Alexander's marriage to Winifred steadies him, while Hilda Burgoyne, an actress from his youth, unsettles him. The bridge he designs becomes a test of nerve and character. An epilogue closes the story after disaster. The short novel shows Cather finding her voice. Cather later called it a study in divided loyalty, and critics still debate its hero.
a-crystal-age:
W. H. Hudson framed A Crystal Age as a romance of the future. his preface admits every such dream is built from the dreamer's own age — in his case, the cults and crazes of the 1880s. His narrator, out botanizing, falls into a ravine, is buried by falling earth, and wakes after a long unconsciousness in a changed world.

The future he finds is a quiet, communal household in a great house amid rich country, where people live close to nature and find his modern habits strange. Love in that ordered world follows rules he cannot accept, and his feeling for a daughter of the house drives the story to its close. Hudson's utopia is pastoral rather than mechanical, a dream of life returned to the soil.
a-straight-deal-or-the-ancient-grudge:
Owen Wister, the novelist of the American West, turns to public argument in nineteen chapters about England and America after the First World War. He begins with the flood of angry letters that any printed opinion now brings. His own opinion is plain: the old grudge between the two peoples should end.

Chapter by chapter he takes up wartime complaints, old history taught badly in schools, Irish questions, and slights remembered on both sides of the Atlantic. He grants faults to each country and asks readers to weigh the record fairly. The book is a plea for friendship between the English-speaking peoples, written in a plain, combative style.
a-treatise-concerning-the-principles-of-:
George Berkeley's Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge inquires into the causes of error in the sciences. Its title page adds the grounds of scepticism, atheism, and irreligion to the charge sheet. Berkeley dedicates the work to the Earl of Pembroke. His preface asks the reader to suspend judgment until the whole is read through once.

Berkeley argues that things exist only as they are perceived by a mind. Matter, as philosophers imagined it, is an empty abstraction behind our ideas. From this he builds proofs of God's existence and the soul's immateriality. An introduction attacks abstract ideas before the principles begin. The treatise made its young Irish author a founder of idealism, the doctrine that reality is mental. Few philosophy books so short have argued so long.
alexander-s-bridge:
Willa Cather's first novel centers on Bartley Alexander, a celebrated bridge builder at the height of his fame. The story opens with Professor Lucius Wilson, who taught Alexander, arriving in Boston and looking up his former student. Wilson's visit frames the portrait of a man whose public triumph rests on a strained marriage and an old love not fully buried.

In ten chapters and an epilogue, Alexander moves between Boston, London, and the great bridge he is building in Canada. A chance reunion with Hilda Burgoyne, the actress he loved before his marriage, reopens what his success had closed. Cather keeps the scale small and the prose exact. This printing also includes Alfred Noyes's poem The Barrel Organ after the novel.
ammianus-marcellinus-roman-history-yonge:
Ammianus Marcellinus, a retired Roman officer, wrote his history of the empire in the late fourth century. C. D. Yonge translated the surviving books into English. Much of the full work is lost, but the remainder is rich.

The surviving books run from Constantius through the reign of Valens. Emperor Julian's Persian campaign receives a long, admiring account from a near witness. Ammianus writes with a soldier's eye for terrain, weather, and morale. Historians rank him as the last great historian of Rome. His pages remain a prime source for the late empire.
amours-de-voyage:
Arthur Hugh Clough wrote his verse tale as a set of letters in English hexameters, and this text follows the 1903 Macmillan edition. The speaker, Claude, travels in Italy while Rome is in turmoil, and writes to his friend Eustace about sights, doubts, and a young woman he keeps meeting. He is clever, restless, and unable to commit to anything.

Across five cantos the letters move from Rome to Florence and the hills, mixing travel notes with shy courtship. Claude questions faith, duty, love, and his own hesitation, often with dry humor. The poem is prized for sounding like real modern thought, unsure and self-mocking, inside old verse forms.
an-inland-voyage:
Robert Louis Stevenson's first book recounts a canoe trip through Belgium and France. His friend Walter Simpson went with him. The dedication addresses Simpson as the Cigarette. The contents chart the route. It runs from Antwerp to Boom, then down the Willebroek Canal. It passes the Royal Sport Nautique and the canalized Sambre, past Maubeuge and Landrecies. At last it follows the Oise in flood, through Compiègne to Précy.

Two young men in canoes are taken for pedlars. Rain soaks them again and again. Innkeepers and canal folk feed and amuse them. Stevenson turns discomfort into comedy. He watches bargemen, lock-keepers, and the flat green country with care. Travel for its own sake is the subject. The book sets out the wandering voice that runs through all his later work.
an-occurrence-at-owl-creek-bridge:
Ambrose Bierce wrote this short story of the Civil War, told in three numbered parts. It opens on a railroad bridge in northern Alabama, where a man stands with a rope around his neck, hands bound, watched by Federal soldiers and a captain. The drop is about to be taken from under his feet. Bierce stays close to the physical facts: the boards, the sentinels, the cannon on the slope.

The condemned man is Peyton Farquhar, a planter who tried to burn the bridge for the Confederacy. As the plank tips, the story follows his sharpening senses and what seems to be an escape through the creek and the woods home. Bierce's ending reframes everything before it, and the tale has become the classic example of the tricked point of view in short fiction.
at-large: At Large, E, w, hornung's raffles tale. The thief at large. This book preserves that story. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
birds-in-town-village:
W. H. Hudson's Birds in Town and Village revises and enlarges his first book about bird life, Birds in a Village, first published in 1893. Hudson rewrote the first portion with fresh observations, threw out matter he judged unworthy, and added an entirely new part on birds in a Cornish village.

Five shorter essays between the two long parts are retained with little alteration, in one or two instances covering the same ground as the new matter. Hudson writes of English rural scenes with the affection of a first book's author, mending faults where he found them. Bird lovers and readers of English nature writing will find this a mellow, observant volume.
by-conduct-and-courage: By Conduct and Courage, G, a, henty's tale, the brave conduct. This book preserves that adventure. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
by-shore-and-sedge:
Bret Harte gathered three California tales in By Shore and Sedge, pieces from the mining frontier he made famous. An Apostle of the Tules opens on a camp meeting in Tasajara Valley in October 1856, four hundred settlers camped in a dreary marsh for a religious revival. Harte watches preachers, sick families, and scoffing boys with his usual mix of irony and pity.

Sarah Walker and A Ship of '49 complete the volume, the last reaching back to the gold rush year itself. Harte's California is a place of sudden gatherings, rough faith, and stranger kindness. These shorter pieces show his method at its purest: a vivid scene, a twist of character, and sentiment kept on a tight rein.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alain-rene-le:
Alain-Rene Le Sage was a writer born at Sarzeau, Morbihan, in 1668, who died at Boulogne-sur-Mer in 1747. Son of a notary who died early, he left the Jesuit college of Vannes penniless, his guardian having squandered his fortune. Marriage came at twenty-six; practised law briefly, then devoted himself to literature.

The Abbe de Lyonne gave him a small pension and encouraged Spanish study. He translated Spanish plays without public favour. His farce Crispin rival de son maitre won marked success in 1707 and stays on the stage. Actors' enmity drove him to the Foire theatre, for which he wrote about a hundred plays. Besides Crispin, Turcaret, Le Diable Boiteux, and Gil Blas deserve special mention. Turcaret ou le Financier, 1709, is a prose comedy about a financier. Gil Blas, despite assertion, is no Spanish plagiarism but an original work counted among France's romance masterpieces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alger-of-lieg:
Alger of Liège, learned French priest born at Liège about 1055, died at Cluny in 1132. He studied at Liège, became Deacon of St. Bartholomew's, and about 1100 Canon of St. Lambert's cathedral, where he stayed twenty years. In 1121 he retired to Cluny's monastery and died there.

His treatise against Berengarius's heresy, De sacramento corporis et sanguinis Domini, won high esteem from Peter of Cluny and Erasmus. His other writings: De misericordia et justitia, a Fathers anthology with brief commentaries, a free-will treatise, and one on the Mass's sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-hallows-c:
All Hallows College prepares priests for the missions in English-speaking countries. In 1840 the young Dublin priest John Hand lived with a Vincentian community, unbound by its rules. He resolved to found a missionary college. The project seemed fanciful for one so young, unknown, and penniless, but Hand trusted Heaven and Irish generosity. He won Gregory XVI's approbation at Rome. With O'Connell's aid he leased a mansion and twenty-six acres north of Dublin, once the Priory of All Hallows' land.

On 1 November 1842, with Archbishop Murray's encouragement, Hand formally opened the college and gave it its present name. For four years he served as president, directing studies, establishing finances, and organizing staff. Then, worn out by labours, above all by collecting funds house to house and parish to parish, he died in the spring of 1846. He left the harvest to others. His ideal was that All Hallows should be apostolic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-ledge:
The altar ledge began as a step raised slightly behind the plain table-shaped altar, holding candlesticks, flowers, reliquaries, and other ornaments. Later the tabernacle joined the altar as a stationary appendage, with further steps at its sides and behind it. These steps are also called degrees or gradini, their fronts sometimes beautifully painted and decorated.

Brunelleschi's Santo Spirito in Florence shows gradini with beautiful miniature groups from the Passion of Christ. The ledge thus marks the altar's growth from bare table to a stepped setting for ornaments and tabernacle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altarage:
Altarage comes from the low Latin altaragium, revenue reserved for the chaplain, or altarist, as against the parish priest's income. The distinction once guarded the chaplain's livelihood apart from the parish priest's own benefice and income. Today it means the fees a priest receives from the laity for functions performed for them, such as marriages, baptisms, funerals, and other rites.

It is also termed honorarium, stipend, stole fee, or altarage itself in modern use. Each name marks the same payment: a free offering for a priest's personal service at life's turning points.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselm-of-lie:
An eleventh-century Belgian chronicler, Anselm of Liège was born in 1008 and died about 1056. Liège's famous episcopal school educated him, and he became canon and dean of the cathedral, where Bishop Wazo was his friend. His chronicle, the Gesta Episcoporum Tungrensium, Trajectensium, et Leodiensium, ranks among the best of its period for literary merit and historical value.

It carries on Heriger of Lobbes's work, which covered the first twenty-seven bishops, from Saint Maternus to Remaclus. Anselm wrote at the request of his godmother, Countess Ida, Abbess of Saint Cecilia at Cologne, adding the lives of twenty-five more bishops, down to Wazo. Wazo gets a very full and particular account. The latest edition of the Gesta appears in Monumenta Germaniae Historica: Scriptores, VII, 161-234, and also XIV, 107-120, from 1883. Anselm's style is clear, and his zeal for church reform matches his critical intelligence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-josep:
Antoine-Joseph Mege, a Maurist Benedictine born at Clermont in 1625, spent his life in prayer, preaching, and study. He joined the Benedictines at Vendome in 1643, taught theology at Saint-Denis, and served as prior at Rethel. Late in life he withdrew to Saint-Germain-des-Pres near Paris, dividing his days between prayer and books.

His chief work commented on the Rule of Saint Benedict, attacking the strict reading of Abbot Rance of La Trappe. Maurist superiors banned the commentary in 1689 at the urging of Bossuet. He also translated Saint Ambrose on virginity and wrote a work on Christian morals, leaving a small but sharp body of monastic writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-berlage:
Anton Berlage, a German dogmatic theologian born at Munster in 1805, taught at his native city's academy until his death in 1881. Early teachers drew him toward risky speculation, but study at Tubingen under Drey, Hirscher, and Mohler turned him to a historical method. Ordained in 1832 without seminary training, he lectured first on apologetics and morals, then on dogma alone.

His seven-volume Catholic Dogmatics, published between 1839 and 1864, gathered his teaching in clear and elegant form. Pupils praised his concise and direct lectures, and his spirit shaped the whole faculty at Munster. The entry presents a teacher whose steady orthodoxy steadied German theology in a restless age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-col:
The Apostolic College means the Twelve Apostles as a body commissioned by Christ to spread the reign of God over the whole world. They are founders, foundation, and supports of the visible church on earth, and the name apostle marks their commission. An apostle is a missionary sent by proper authority to carry the gospel to new lands, a meaning fixed by the sending of the Twelve. To call them a college implies they worked together under one head for one purpose.

Referring readers to the article on Apostles for scriptural treatment, this entry deals with dogmatic aspects, the doctrines behind accredited envoys and teachers. Christ, it argues, founded a teaching, governing, and serving apostolate whose charter lies in the gospel commissions. The piece suits readers who want the theology behind the Twelve, not just their names and stories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-banns-of-marr:
Banns of marriage are the church's public announcement of the names of people planning to marry. The word comes from Latin bannum and Old English bannan, to summon. Their object is to uncover any impediment to the marriage and to tell all interested parties of its near celebration. From Christian society's start, marriage counted as a public religious act under church control.

Notice to the bishop dates to the second century, and later the parish priest took up the duty with reputable parishioners' help. Publishing names in church seems to have begun in France near the end of the twelfth century. It was already Gallican custom in 1215, when Innocent III mentioned it to Beauvais's bishop. That same year the Fourth Lateran Council made banns a general law of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-age:
Canonical age is the year fixed by church law at which a person becomes able to take on duties. He may enjoy privileges, enter states of life, hold office, or receive sacraments. Each such act needs growth of mind and body fitted to free acceptance, with knowledge of its duties. The Church sets the age at which one is generally thought qualified. Less growth suffices for baptism than for marriage or priesthood, and higher offices demand more.

Jurists split life into seven ages. They are infancy to seven, childhood to fourteen, puberty to twenty-five, and majority to forty. Manhood runs to fifty or sixty, old age to seventy, and decrepitude to a hundred or death, each year complete. Old discipline varied by time and place. Gratian set seven for tonsure and the first minor orders, twelve for acolyte, twenty for subdeaconship, and thirty for deaconship, later 25.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carthage:
Carthage was a Phoenician colony that long rivaled Rome for mastery of the civilized world before a Roman army destroyed it in 146 B.C. Julius Caesar refounded it in 44 B.C. as a Roman colony, and it became capital of Africa Nova, a province that grew rich and flourishing. African Christianity opens in 180 with martyrs at Scillium and Madaura, and within twenty years a thriving church stood at Carthage.

Tertullian, born at Carthage about 160, defended the faith in his Apology of about 197, claiming Christians had filled every corner of African life. Cyprian, elected bishop in 249, stands with Tertullian as the great figure of the early church there. Later sections trace the primacy of Carthage, its councils, and its bishops. Leo XIII restored the archdiocese in 1884 under Cardinal Lavigerie, who revived Christian life on the ancient site.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-dufre:
Charles Dufresne du Cange was a historian and philologist born at Amiens in 1610 and dead at Paris in 1688. His father, a magistrate, had him taught by the Jesuits at Amiens. He studied law at Orléans and joined the Bar before the Parlement of Paris in 1631. The law did not satisfy him, so he returned to Amiens, married in 1638, and in 1645 bought his father-in-law's post as Treasurer of France.

Neither office nor a family of ten children kept him from scholarship. Conversant with many languages, he was consulted from all sides and gathered much through correspondence. His energy went largely to the history of France and of Constantinople. Two great works grew from that preparation, above all his glossary of medieval and late Latin writers, published at Paris in three folio volumes in 1678.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-b:
An entry on Christopher Bainbridge, Archbishop of York and cardinal, born near Appleby about 1464. He entered Queen's College, Oxford, became its provost before 1495 and a doctor of laws, and later gave generously to the college. He held many benefices, including the London treasurership and the Mastership of the Rolls. Henry the Seventh named him Bishop of Durham in 1507, and the pope moved him to York in 1508.

Sent by Henry the Eighth as ambassador to Rome in 1509, Bainbridge was made cardinal by Julius the Second in March 1511 for winning Henry to the pope against France. He led a papal expedition that besieged Ferrara with success, and he sought the title Most Christian King for Henry after Louis of France forfeited it. In July 1514 his steward, the priest Rinaldo de Modena, poisoned him in revenge for a blow, and Bainbridge was buried in the English Hospice at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cities-of-ref:
The cities of refuge were towns where Jewish law gave asylum to anyone who had killed another without intent, sheltering him from the avenger of blood. Under blood-revenge, a victim's kinsman held it a duty to kill the slayer, intentional or not. The six biblical cities were Cedes in Galilee, Sichem in Mount Ephraim, and Hebron in the south, west of Jordan, with Bosor, Ramoth in Galaad, and Gaulon in Basan to the east.

Three western cities seem to have come first, probably under Josias, with the eastern three added when Jews spread wider after the Exile. Protection was conditional: the fugitive had to prove his deed unpremeditated, then stay within the city's bounds, unable to return home or buy off the avenger. An intentional killer found no refuge even at God's altar, and might be dragged from it to death, as Joab was.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-marriag:
In municipal law marriage is not a contract in the strict sense but a civil status. It unites one man and one woman legally for life, with rights and duties assigned by the law of matrimony. It is presumed to serve the State's highest interest, so the law encourages it, holds it permanent, and dissolves it only by death or, where statutes allow, by divorce. Consent of the parties is essential to a valid marriage.

In England solemnisation before a clergyman was required until 1836, except for Quakers and Jews, when civil and dissenter marriages were legalised. Common-law ages of consent were fourteen for males and twelve for females, and the act of 1753 voided underage marriages lacking parental consent. The article surveys formalities, annulment for deception or duress, and foreign rules, from Scotland's irregular marriages by mere consent to Germany's higher ages and Quebec's parental consent under twenty-one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college:
Robert Schwickerath's wide survey starts from the word college itself, from the Latin collegium. At first it meant a community, a corporation, or a body of colleagues in a common pursuit. Rome knew guilds of artisans as collegia, plus groups joined for worship or mutual aid. Official bodies bore the name too, such as the College of Pontiffs. The sense survives in modern bodies like the College of Physicians and the College of Surgeons.

From the fourteenth century the word often meant a community of secular clergy living on a foundation for religious service. Schwickerath treats England, where the collegiate system still marks Oxford and Cambridge, and notes Winchester College, founded in 1379 as the first college outside a university. He follows the humanist influence, the colleges of Paris, and the American college, long the main home of liberal education and now in a state of transition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concubinage:
H. A. Gaynor's entry defines concubinage today as a more or less permanent state of a man and woman living in illicit intercourse. Strictly it covers unions where neither party is bound by vow, marriage, Holy Orders, or kinship. Dwelling together does not matter. Repetition or continuance of illicit relations between the same persons forms the essence. The term, however, has not always meant the same thing.

In the Old Testament a legitimate spouse of lower rank, or a bondwoman, might be called concubine without denying her marriage. The label marked her lesser share in rank, property, and household rule. Roman law and early church records used a like sense: a quasi-wife, recognized by law under set terms. Toledo's council of 400 legislated for laymen on the matter. With Rome's fall and Roman law's decline, lawful concubinage faded, and the word took its modern illicit sense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-o:
This reference entry covers two councils held at Orange in southern France, the first in 441 and the second in 529, and explains why the second matters far beyond its region. It sets each meeting in its place, names its president and bishops, and lists the subjects its canons addressed.

The first council, under Hilary of Arles, issued thirty canons on the sacraments, sanctuary, relations among bishops, catechumens, and the marriage of clergy. Far more important was the second council, presided over by Caesarius of Arles, the first in Gaul to issue a decision on a matter of faith. Its rulings on grace and free will shaped Western teaching for centuries, and the entry points readers to the acts and modern studies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deluge:
A long scriptural entry treats the Deluge, the catastrophe fully described in Genesis chapters 6 to 9 and recalled across Scripture from Wisdom to Second Peter. It considers the biblical account, its historicity, the Flood's universality, and collateral questions in turn. Genesis tells how God, seeing human wickedness, spared Noah's family, commanded an ark, and sent forty days' rain, with waters prevailing 150 days.

Critics read the account as a mosaic of two flood stories, Yahwistic and Priestly, differing in authorship and detail. Historicity weighs four theories, from mere fancy to borrowing, against flood legends worldwide. Universality asks whether the Flood covered the whole earth or destroyed all men over part of it. Time, place, and natural causes follow, with dates from rival texts and Babylonian parallels in the Tigris-Euphrates valley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demiurge:
A philosophy entry defines the demiurge, literally a public worker, a word first used for any craftsman serving the public. Soon other words took the common artisan, while demiurge was reserved for the Great Artificer, the Architect of the universe. At first writers added of the world to distinguish him, but gradually demiurge alone meant the Maker of heaven and earth, as in Plato's Timaeus.

Strictly the word never meant one producing from nothing, for which Greeks used ktistes, but only a maker who shapes and models given matter. Heathen philosophy always presupposes matter, and its world-maker need not be the supreme God. In Gnosticism the Demiurge became a central figure. He stands apart from the Supreme God, and often hostile to him, as the flawed maker of the material world. Other writings, by contrast, identify him with the Highest God himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
An ecclesiastical judge is a churchman holding church jurisdiction, whether in the broad sense or the strict. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that the official body set by lawful authority to administer justice is called a court, tribunal, or audience. Every court holds at least two sworn officers, the judge who decides and the clerk who keeps the record of proceedings and judgment.

As a rule, however, a church court forms a collegiate tribunal, whose members either join the president in deciding as judges or advise him as councillors and assessors. The entry cites Hergenrother-Hollweck, Laurentius, and Sagmuller on the shape of church courts. It gives students of canon law the personnel of justice in short compass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-james-c:
Henry James Coleridge, a writer and preacher born in Devonshire in 1822, was grandson of the poet's brother, son of a King's Bench judge. After Eton and a career at Trinity and Oriel, Oxford, he took Anglican orders in 1848 and joined the Tractarian ranks and helped start The Guardian as the High Church organ. Shaken by Newman's secession, the Gorham judgment, and the condemnations of Pusey and Ward, he was received into the Catholic Church in 1852 after a retreat at Clapham.

Ordained in 1856, Coleridge entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1857 and in 1865 became the Jesuit editor of The Month, adding The Messenger in 1877. He projected the Quarterly Series and wrote The Public Life of Our Lord, lives of Francis Xavier and Teresa, and the gospel harmony Vita Vitae Nostrae. Failing health forced his resignation from The Month in 1881, and after a seizure in 1890 he finished his work at Roehampton before dying in 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-ma:
This article treats marriage chiefly as a lasting condition, with its moral and social aspects, rather than as a mere ceremony. Marriage is usually defined as the legitimate union of husband and wife. Legitimate means sanctioned by natural, evangelical, or civil law, and husband and wife implies mutual rights, life in common, and an enduring bond. Those last marks set marriage apart from concubinage and fornication.

The definition is broad enough to cover polygamous and polyandrous unions allowed by civil law. The theory of primitive promiscuity, debated by writers from 1860 to 1890, finds little support in historical times. The entry then weighs deviations from marriage. It argues that Christianity gave the world its highest ideal of unadulterated monogamy, with equality between the two parties, an influence spreading far beyond Christian lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-lamy-b: Jérôme Lamy Besange, born at Linz in 1726 and dead in 1781, taught Scripture at Salzburg for twenty-four years. His published works are an Introduction to the Old Testament in two volumes, an Introduction to the Four Gospels, an Introduction to the Acts of the Apostles. There is also a commentary on the Passion called Fasciculus Myrrhae, and a rendering of the seven penitential psalms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-lafarge:
John LaFarge was an American painter, decorator, and writer who revolutionized stained glass. Born in New York in 1835 to a French naval officer father, he studied at Mount St. Mary's and Fordham, meant to study law, but after Paris study with Couture turned to art. His early Newport landscapes already showed originality in color values and the influence of Japanese art, which he pioneered studying.

Experimenting with color, he rivaled medieval windows. He added new resources by inventing opalescent glass and methods of superimposing and welding it, seen in the Battle Window at Harvard and the Peacock Window at Worcester. His mural work began at Trinity Church, Boston, in 1873, and in his seventy-first year he painted lunettes on the history of religion for the St. Paul capitol. His books on painting, Japan, and the masters matched a wide-ranging mind.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-st-mary: Mount St. Mary's in Emmitsburg, Maryland, is one of America's oldest Catholic seminaries, founded in 1808 amid the Catoctin Mountains. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-marr: Mystical marriage is the soul's highest union with God, described by the saints as a spiritual betrothal. childe-harold-s-pilgrimage:
Lord Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage is a long poem in four cantos, addressed first to Ianthe. A dedication in verse praises the young girl's guileless heart before Harold appears. The pilgrim himself is a satiated young lord who leaves England to wander. Spain and Portugal, fresh from Peninsular war, fill the first canto.

Greece under Turkish rule fills the second, with lament for her fallen glory. The third canto crosses Waterloo's field to Switzerland, Byron's own exile written into Harold's. The fourth wanders Italy: Venice, Florence, and Rome in decay. Byron published the cantos over six years and woke famous after the first. Harold's gloom became the Byronic hero, copied across Europe. The poem mixes travel description, history, and confession in Spenserian stanzas of sustained splendour, and it made modern tourism melancholy.
cicero-de-natura-deorum-yonge:
Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods, written in 45 BC, stages a debate on religion among Rome's educated elite. C. D. Yonge's translation, from the Harper edition of 1877, is the text here. Cicero sets the scene at a friend's villa and mostly listens.

An Epicurean speaker argues the gods exist but care nothing for human affairs. A Stoic answers that divine reason runs the world and watches over it. An Academic skeptic then takes both cases apart, finding each one wanting. The dialogue is the fullest surviving survey of ancient thought on the gods, and its balance made it a school text for centuries.
cicero-philippics-yonge:
Cicero's Philippics are fourteen speeches against Mark Antony, delivered in 44 and 43 BC after the murder of Julius Caesar. C. D. Yonge's English translation is the text here, drawn from the fourth volume of his Orations. Cicero named them after Demosthenes' speeches against Philip of Macedon.

An old man with no army, Cicero used speech alone to brand Antony a public enemy and rally the Senate against him. The gamble worked for a season, then failed: the triumvirs proscribed him, and Antony had him killed in December 43 BC. The speeches are his last stand for the republic. They cost him his life and fixed his fame.
cicero-tusculan-disputations-yonge:
Cicero wrote the Tusculan Disputations in 45 BC at his villa in Tusculum, in the last stretch of his career. C. D. Yonge's English translation is the text here. The work holds five days of talk with friends on how to face life's hardest blows.

Each day takes one fear: death, pain, grief, the passions of the soul, and the question whether virtue alone makes a happy life. Cicero argues death is no evil, pain can be borne, and grief yields to reason. His answers lean Stoic, though he keeps his Academic freedom to doubt. The talks became a handbook of calm for later ages.
diary-of-a-pilgrimage:

Along the way he complains of phrasebooks full of raspberries, figs, and medlars no traveler ever wants. The diary mixes farce and genuine feeling in the proportion that made Jerome beloved.

english-men-of-letters-coleridge:
H. D. Traill's Coleridge, from the English Men of Letters series, attempts a short life and critical estimate of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. Traill quotes De Quincey's warning that Coleridge's multiform attainments make enormous demands on any biographer, and he admits the shortcomings his narrow limits impose.

No complete biography of Coleridge on an important scale then existed, Traill notes, and no critical appreciation had yet correlated the whole work with the changes of his life. His volume tries to do both in brief: the poet, philosopher and talker, and the circumstances that shaped him. Readers meeting Coleridge for the first time will find Traill a sane, readable guide to a famously difficult man.
faxian-record-buddhistic-kingdoms-legge:
Faxian, a Chinese Buddhist monk, recorded his pilgrimage to India in 414 CE. James Legge translated the Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms into English. Faxian had walked from China through Central Asia between 399 and 414.

He crossed deserts and mountains seeking complete texts of monastic rules. Kingdoms, monasteries, and relics of the Buddha fill his spare narrative. Storms at sea nearly ended his return voyage with his books. The record is the earliest surviving Chinese travel narrative of its kind. Legge's translation trails him past countries now transformed or gone. Adventure and devotion combine in Faxian's calm, factual voice throughout.
framley-parsonage:
Anthony Trollope continues the Barsetshire chronicles in this novel of the vicar of Framley. Mark Robarts holds the living of Framley through the patronage of Lady Lufton, whose son Lord Lufton is his closest friend. The contents open with the two sets of the county, the Framley set and the Chaldicotes set, between which the young clergyman must steer.

Robarts is flattered into the faster company of Mr. Sowerby and signs bills he cannot pay. Debt pulls him toward disgrace while his wife Fanny holds the household together. Lady Lufton's opposition to her son's marriage to Lucy Robarts, the vicar's sister, runs as the second thread. Trollope lets money, patronage, and clerical pride do the damage, and rescue comes slowly and at a price.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BernauGeorgePro: Gary Hart, the Colorado senator with a lifelong interest in the Kennedy era, is the reviewer in this file: his subject is 'Promises to Keep' by George Bernau. The document preserves the review as released, a senator's published judgment on a book from the Kennedy literature that fills this archive. It is kept as issued, one of the many press pieces gathered by the researchers who collected everything the case produced in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ColumbiaCollege:
In April 1970 Harold Weisberg quarreled by mail with Mirron Alexandroff, president of Columbia College in Chicago. The subject was Sherman Skolnick, the Chicago researcher, whom Weisberg accused of plagiarizing his materials in a federal court filing.

Skolnick taught and broadcast in Chicago and drew on the case's literature freely, and Weisberg guarded his documents with famous jealousy. The letters show the movement's internal policing: credit and theft argued out, with a college president drawn into the exchange. It sits in Weisberg's files as an unusually formal record of a researchers' feud, argued on letterheads.
